text.p: NASA said on Monday it was delaying Friday's planned launch of shuttle Columbia by at least a week to allow more time to study a puzzling booster rocket problem that cropped up on the last shuttle flight.
Engineers want to better understand what caused deep gouges in the protective insulation that lined the bell-shaped nozzle of one of two solid rocket boosters used by shuttle Atlantis in September.
Columbia was scheduled to blastoff on a 16-day science mission on Friday, but the launch will take place no earlier than on Nov. 15, said NASA spokesman James Hartsfield.

"The investigation team seems to be reaching a point where they have a good understanding of the phenomenon, but an extra week will make sure they are not rushed and can present the results in the best possible way," he said.
Space agency engineers have conducted more than a thousand tests to determine what caused about 60 half-inch-deep gouges in the rocket nozzle insulation.
"The erosion was not a danger, but nevertheless it was more than we had seen before in 79 shuttle launches," said Hartsfield. "We feel we need a better understanding of the phenomenon."

NASA Administrator Daniel Goldin last week formed a three-member independent team to review the space agency's investigation work. That team did not influence the decision to delay Columbia's launch, according to Hartsfield.

The solid rocket boosters, which provide most of the shuttle's thrust during the first two minutes of launch, are considered the most dangerous components of the multi-billion dollar vehicle. It was a leaking rocket booster that caused the 1986 Challenger disaster.
Columbia's crew of five, which had been due to arrive at Florida's Kennedy Space Centre on Monday evening, will stay at the Johnson Space Centre in Houston to wait out the delay.
During the 16-day mission, the astronauts are due to release and later retrieve a pair of science satellites, and make two spacewalks to study space station construction techniques.
